text: Meet TradeShock S K. Saskatchewan grain farms plan next year's crops in winter, but a single trade headline, like new duties on canola, can wreck that plan. TradeShock stress-tests your crop plan against the headline, before you buy seed.

Start with your farm: soil zone, acres, the crops you grow, and simple rotation limits. A linear-programming optimizer builds the most profitable crop mix, using the Saskatchewan Ministry of Agriculture's 2026 Crop Planning Guide, checked line by line.

Trade Watch automates the scanning. It reads official Government of Canada news, flags the trade items, and stress-tests each one against your farm, ranked by dollar impact. This is a hypothetical demo feed.
One click turns a headline into a scenario: which crops are hit, by how much, how confident, and a bear-to-bull range. Every estimate is a slider, so the farmer always has the final say.

The optimizer re-plans instantly. Keeping the old plan would drop returns to about three hundred and five thousand dollars. Re-planning lifts it back to three hundred and fifty-eight thousand. That's fifty-three thousand dollars left on the table if you don't adjust.
Not sure about the estimate? Drag a slider, and the whole plan updates in real time.

text: Bear, base, and bull cases show which plan holds up whichever way prices go, and how much you would regret each choice.

The risk lens replays one hundred and forty real price moves and thirty-five real harvest years from Statistics Canada, including the 2021 drought. It shows how bad a bad year can get, and a crop mix that cushions it.

Farmers can simply ask: what if peas drop twenty percent and I cap canola at twenty-five percent? With live AI, Claude answers by calling the optimizer as tools, so every number is computed, not guessed. Here, offline mode answers the same question with built-in rules.
A plain-English summary and a one-page PDF are ready for your lender or agronomist. It's a planning aid, not financial advice.
